scenario.description: A lead trial attorney must approve the company's response to broad document requests in a trade-secret lawsuit, including production scope, customer-data treatment, employee-record handling, and the use of a forensic expert, with input from discovery counsel, the client liaison, privacy counsel, and insurance counsel.

shared_context.S1: The company is defending a trade-secret lawsuit in state court.
shared_context.S2: The plaintiff has served requests seeking source code, customer records, internal communications, and personnel files.
shared_context.S3: The court's case-management order requires the company's first production within 21 days.
shared_context.S4: The current draft discovery plan proposes producing the responsive material under a protective order and hiring a forensic expert to collect data from company systems.
shared_context.S5: At the weekly discovery sign-off, Elena asks discovery, the client liaison, privacy, and insurance counsel for their recommendations before approving the production plan.

PF1.text: While completing a supplemental review of the source-code repository yesterday, Thomas confirmed that exactly 17 files responsive to the requests contain third-party licensed code covered by confidentiality restrictions. Those restrictions cannot be satisfied by the existing protective order alone, so the correct production decision is to withhold exactly these 17 files from production. He has not entered that result in the discovery matrix yet.

PF2.text: During a client call this week, the company's chief customer officer instructed Nadia that customer names must not appear in the production and that responsive customer records should use anonymized customer identifiers; the instruction has not yet been added to the written discovery instructions.

PF3.text: Wei's privacy scan of the personnel collection found exactly 42 records containing personal identifiers of employees in the European Union; those identifiers must be redacted, and the production may include only aggregate employee information from those records.

PF4.text: James confirmed from the applicable defense-policy endorsement that the carrier must approve the forensic expert's collection protocol at least 5 business days before any forensic image is taken; this requirement is not reflected in the current draft plan.

acceptance_conditions: Exactly 17 third-party licensed files must be withheld from production.
Customer names must not be produced and customer identifiers must be anonymized.
Identifiers in exactly 42 EU employee records must be redacted, with only aggregate employee information produced from those records.
Carrier approval must be obtained before forensic imaging, at least 5 business days in advance.
The plan must include a commitment whose detail states that carrier approval is required before forensic imaging at least 5 business days in advance.
Thomas's discovery finding must be cited as a justification for the production plan.

content_checks.C7: decisions['carrier_approval_before_forensic_imaging'] == True and decisions['carrier_approval_lead_days'] == 5 and any('carrier' in c['detail'] and ('5 business days' in c['detail'] or '5-business-day' in c['detail']) for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: The broad requests and existing protective order would otherwise support producing the responsive source-code files, but this finding establishes that exactly 17 files must instead be withheld because the protective order alone cannot satisfy their confidentiality restrictions.
The client instruction changes the customer-data treatment from ordinary production of identified records to no customer names and anonymized identifiers.
The privacy scan changes the handling of exactly 42 EU employee records from ordinary production to redaction of identifiers in 42 records and aggregate employee information only.
The policy endorsement changes the forensic plan by requiring carrier approval at least 5 business days before imaging and requires a commitment documenting that carrier-approval step.
